The Supreme Covenant
Promulgation at Uhuru Park27 August 2010
Preamble of Kenya
“We, the people of Kenya, ACKNOWLEDGING the supremacy of the Almighty God of all creation; HONOURING those who heroically struggled to bring freedom and justice to our land... EXERCISING our sovereign and inalienable right to determine the form of governance of our country... ADOPT, ENACT and give this Constitution to ourselves and to our future generations.”
Uhuru Park, NairobiPromulgated August 27, 2010
Historical Trajectory

The Long March to The 2010 Katiba

From colonial marginalization and imperial centralization to citizen defiance and formal promulgation at Uhuru Park.

1920s to 1963Lancaster House

Colonial Legacy and Independence Compromise

British colonial rule utilized a divide and rule strategy that marginalized various communities. During negotiations for the 1963 Independence Constitution at Lancaster House, smaller ethnic communities feared domination by larger groups. The British brokered a compromise that included a bicameral parliament and regionalism to diffuse power. Kenya gained independence in 1963.

1964 to 1989One-Party Era

The Rise of the Imperial Presidency

The ruling elite viewed regionalism as a threat to national unity and state resources. A series of rapid amendments dismantled the regional assemblies and abolished the Senate in 1968. The roles of Head of State and Government were merged. In 1982, a constitutional amendment officially made Kenya a de jure one party state. The government suppressed political dissent, independent courts, and civil society.

1990 to 1997Section 2A Repeal

The Second Liberation

The fall of the Berlin Wall shifted global geopolitics, and international donors tied economic aid to democratic reforms. A coalition of clergy, lawyers, academics, and veteran politicians launched the Saba Saba movement. Facing domestic riots and the suspension of foreign aid, the government repealed Section 2A in 1991 to allow multi party politics. Parliament later passed the Constitution of Kenya Review Commission Act in 1997.

1998 to 2004Bomas Conference

Civil Society Push and the Bomas Draft

Civil society organizations, religious groups, and citizens demanded a citizen led constitutional review. The National Constitutional Conference convened at the Bomas of Kenya auditorium in Nairobi in 2003. This representative assembly produced the Bomas Draft in 2004, focusing on devolution and clipping executive power to prevent dictatorship.

2005Wako Draft Rejected

Political Betrayal and the First Referendum

The government altered the Bomas Draft to create the Wako Draft, retaining a powerful central presidency. The 2005 referendum became a proxy political war. Kenyans overwhelmingly rejected the Wako Draft.

2007 to 2010National Accord

The Breaking Point and National Survival

The failure to enact a new constitution left the centralized presidential system intact for the 2007 general elections. Disputed election results triggered post election violence that left over 1,000 dead and hundreds of thousands displaced. The 2008 National Accord mandated comprehensive constitutional reform to address historical grievances. Parliament established a Committee of Experts in 2008 to harmonize previous drafts.

2010National Referendum

The 2010 Referendum Campaigns

The new draft constitution faced a national referendum in August 2010 with two primary factions. The Green or Yes Camp secured 68.6% of the national vote. President Mwai Kibaki and Prime Minister Raila Odinga united to lead the campaign in favor of the new constitution. Vice President Kalonzo Musyoka and Water Minister Charity Ngilu campaigned for the Yes vote in the lower Eastern Province. The Red or No Camp garnered 31.4% of the national vote. Higher Education Minister William Ruto served as the primary political spokesman and leader of the No campaign, successfully rallying the Rift Valley Province against the proposed constitution. A coalition of Christian clergy formed a massive bloc within the No camp, campaigning against the draft because it enshrined Kadhi courts into the Constitution.

Referendum Results:
Yes Camp68.6%
No Camp31.4%
August 27, 2010Uhuru Park Promulgation

Promulgation

President Mwai Kibaki formally promulgated the new Constitution at Uhuru Park in Nairobi. The document officially cements this legacy by HONOURING those who heroically struggled to bring freedom and justice to our land and acknowledging that the Kenyan people participated fully in the making of this Constitution.

The Historical Consensus

The 2010 Constitution was forged through decades of civic resistance, constitutional conferences, and democratic sacrifice. It replaced an imperial presidency with devolved self-governance, independent oversight, and justiciable civil liberties.

Constitutional chapters

Structured summaries and article directories for all 18 chapters of the Constitution of Kenya (2010).

1

Sovereignty of the People and Supremacy of this Constitution

Mamlaka ya Wananchi na Ukuu wa Katiba HiiArticles 1 to 3

Declares that all sovereign power belongs to the people of Kenya, to be exercised directly or through democratically elected representatives. Establishes the Constitution as the supreme law binding all persons and State organs.

2

The Republic

Jamhuri ya KenyaArticles 4 to 11

Defines Kenya as a multi-party democratic state founded on national values including democracy, rule of law, human rights, devolution, and integrity.

3

Citizenship

UraiaArticles 12 to 18

Outlines rights and duties of Kenyan citizens, acquisition of citizenship by birth or registration, dual citizenship rights, and retention of nationality.

4

The Bill of Rights

Haki na Uhuru wa MsingiArticles 19 to 59

An integral part of Kenya's democratic state and the framework for social, economic, and cultural policies. Protects civil liberties, socio-economic entitlements, and marginalized groups.

5

Land and Environment

Ardhi na MazingiraArticles 60 to 72

Classifies land into public, community, and private categories. Mandates equitable access, security of land rights, sustainable management, and elimination of gender discrimination in land law.

6

Leadership and Integrity

Uongozi na MaadiliArticles 73 to 80

Establishes that public office is a trust to be exercised with honor, dignity, and accountability to the people. Sets strict standards against conflicts of interest and corruption.

7

Representation of the People

Uwakilishi wa WananchiArticles 81 to 92

Governs the electoral system, general principles of voting, voter registration, political parties, and the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC).

8

The Legislature

BungeArticles 93 to 128

Establishes a bicameral Parliament comprising the National Assembly and the Senate. Details lawmaking processes, legislative oversight, and impeachment procedures.

9

The Executive

Serikali KuuArticles 129 to 158

Structures the Executive comprising the President, Deputy President, and Cabinet Secretaries. Eliminates imperial presidency and subjects appointments to parliamentary vetting.

10

Judiciary

Idara ya MahakamaArticles 159 to 173

Guarantees judicial independence, establishes the Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, High Court, and Judicial Service Commission to prevent executive interference.

11

Devolved Government

Serikali za UgatuziArticles 174 to 200

Establishes 47 County Governments to decentralize state functions, distribute national resources equitably, and give communities direct control of local development.

12

Public Finance

Fedha za UmmaArticles 201 to 231

Establishes principles of openness, accountability, and equitable public expenditure. Creates the Office of the Controller of Budget and Auditor-General.

13

The Public Service

Utumishi wa UmmaArticles 232 to 237

Establishes values of professional ethics, merit-based appointments, transparent service delivery, and the Public Service Commission.

14

National Security

Usalama wa KitaifaArticles 238 to 247

Regulates national security organs: Kenya Defence Forces (KDF), National Intelligence Service (NIS), and National Police Service (NPS). Subjects security forces to civilian authority and human rights standards.

15

Commissions and Independent Offices

Tume na Ofisi HuruArticles 248 to 254

Protects constitutional democracy by establishing independent watchdogs immune from direction or control by the executive or any other authority.

16

Amendment of this Constitution

Kufanya Marekebisho kwenye Katiba HiiArticles 255 to 257

Establishes stringent safeguards against arbitrary constitutional mutilation. Requires mandatory national referenda for core sovereign provisions.

17

General Provisions

Masharti ya JumlaArticles 258 to 260

Provides judicial enforcement rules for constitutional claims, definitions, and interpretive guidelines for courts.

18

Transitional and Consequential Provisions

Masharti ya Mpito na MatokeoArticles 261 to 264

Sets the statutory schedule for enacting implementing legislation, repealing the former 1963 Constitution, and managing the transition to devolved governance.

The story of our Constitution

  • •Prior to 2010, the 1963 independence constitution suffered excessive amendments.
  • •Centralized presidential power governed with weak checks and balances.
  • •Widespread human rights violations prompted pro-democracy movements in the 1990s.

Request parameters

Official citizen petitionAccess to Information Act, 2016
2026-10-27
FORMAL REQUEST FOR ACCESS TO INFORMATION
PURSUANT TO ARTICLE 35 OF THE CONSTITUTION OF KENYA, 2010
AND THE ACCESS TO INFORMATION ACT (NO. 31 OF 2016)

Date: 2026-10-27

TO:
The County Chief Officer / Designated Information Officer,
Department of Finance and Economic Planning,
County Government of Nairobi City County,
Republic of Kenya.

FROM:
Name of Applicant: [Your Full Name]
National ID Number: [Your ID Number]
Email: [Your Email Address]
Telephone: [Your Phone Number]

RE: FORMAL REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INFORMATION UNDER ARTICLE 35

Dear Sir/Madam,

1. Pursuant to Article 35(1)(a) of the Constitution of Kenya, which guarantees that "Every citizen has the right of access to information held by the State", read together with Sections 4 and 8 of the Access to Information Act (No. 31 of 2016), I hereby respectfully request copies of the following information:

REQUEST DETAILS:
Detailed breakdown of the FY 2023/2024 County Ward Development Fund expenditures and procurement tenders awarded for local health centers.

2. In accordance with Section 9 of the Access to Information Act, 2016, a public entity is mandated to respond to an application within twenty-one (21) days of receipt.

3. I look forward to your timely response in the public interest and in defense of good governance and accountability as enshrined under Article 10 of our Constitution.

Yours faithfully,

[Your Signature & Full Name]
Citizen of the Republic of Kenya
Statutory notice: Section 9 of the Access to Information Act mandates a response within 21 calendar days.
